claims.text: The persistence of structural and chemical stability in initially disordered, single-phase high-entropy nanoparticles is governed by the degree of local lattice distortion.
Strong local lattice distortion induces sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish atomic diffusion kinetically hinders the thermodynamic drive for phase separation, short-range ordering, and secondary-precipitate formation.
Weak local distortion relative to the thermodynamic driving force permits high-temperature diffusion, chemical reordering, and precipitation.
Unfavorable mixing enthalpies between particular elemental pairs create a thermodynamic drive for phase separation.
Severe lattice distortion creates a rugged energy landscape that reduces atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses the formation and growth of chemically ordered clusters and secondary phases at elevated temperatures.
When lattice distortion is insufficient, atomic diffusion facilitates the evolution of short-range order or precipitates.
Nanoparticles with sufficiently high local lattice distortion will remain single-phase and show negligible short-range order or secondary-phase formation throughout 473–1923 K.
Retention of the single-phase state will preserve catalytic and thermoelectric properties.
Nanoparticles with lower effective lattice distortion will develop measurable chemical ordering, precipitates, or lattice-parameter shifts during prolonged thermal exposure.
Ordering and phase separation in low-distortion nanoparticles will be especially apparent near the upper end of the 473–1923 K range.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are assumed to be disordered, single-phase solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have high catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticle size and surface-energy effects can alter atomic diffusion kinetics.
Surface oxidation and environmental impurities can affect stability independently of intrinsic lattice distortion.
Thermal exposure at 473 K, 900 K, and 1923 K can be used to compare nanoparticles engineered to have high and low local lattice distortion.
Formation of ordered clusters, secondary precipitates, or compositional segregation in the high-distortion group under minimized extrinsic effects would contradict the proposed stability mechanism.

contradictions.description: The two sets are specified to have identical overall compositions, but minor compositional tuning is simultaneously proposed as a way to create their different lattice distortions.

The conditions assume nanometer-scale samples for which surface-to-volume effects are minimal relative to bulk diffusion, while the boundary and uncertainty fields acknowledge that nanoparticle size and surface-energy effects may substantially alter diffusion kinetics.
